explanations: CompTIA's six-step troubleshooting methodology: (1) Identify the problem: gather information, question users, back up data, (2) Establish a theory of probable cause: question the obvious, (3) Test the theory: confirm or re-establish theory, (4) Establish a plan of action, and implement the solution, (5) Verify full system functionality, and implement preventive measures, (6) Document findings, actions, and outcomes. Review: Chapter 11, Troubleshooting Methodology.

In Task Manager, sorting by CPU usage reveals which process is consuming resources. The process "svchost_update.exe" at 94% CPU is the culprit, and the suspicious name (mimicking svchost.exe) suggests it could be malware. Legitimate svchost.exe runs from C:\Windows\System32. After ending the task, investigate the file location and run a malware scan. Review: Chapter 11, Troubleshooting Methodology (Task Manager, performance monitoring, identifying resource hogs).

netstat -an displays all connections (-a) in numeric format (-n, showing IP addresses instead of hostnames). The -n flag speeds up output by skipping DNS resolution. Adding -o shows the owning process ID. Look for unexpected ESTABLISHED connections to unknown external IPs or unusual LISTENING ports that could indicate a backdoor. Review: Chapter 6, Introduction to TCP/IP (netstat, network monitoring, port analysis).

One long beep followed by three short beeps is a classic IBM/legacy POST code for a video adapter failure. The system can't initialize the display, so the screen stays black and the error is communicated via beep codes. Common causes: GPU not seated properly, auxiliary power cable not connected, or dead GPU. Memory failures typically produce continuous short beeps or a different pattern. Review: Chapter 11, Troubleshooting Methodology (POST, beep codes, BIOS error codes, no-display troubleshooting).

tracert (traceroute on Linux/Mac) sends ICMP packets with incrementing TTL values to map every router hop between your machine and the destination. Each hop shows three round-trip times, making it easy to identify where latency increases. A sudden jump in response time or timeouts (***) indicates a problem at that hop or ISP segment. Review: Chapter 6, Introduction to TCP/IP (tracert, network path analysis, latency troubleshooting).

To boot from USB, change "Boot Option #1" from the current hard drive to the USB device. In most BIOS/UEFI interfaces, you select the boot priority option and choose the USB drive from the list. Some systems also support a one-time boot menu (usually F12) that lets you select a boot device without permanently changing the order. Review: Chapter 1, Motherboards, Processors, and Memory (BIOS/UEFI boot configuration, boot order, USB boot).

If the image is visible under a flashlight but the screen appears dark, the LCD panel is working but the backlight has failed. In older laptops, this was the CCFL inverter; in modern LED-backlit displays, it's the LED driver circuit or the LEDs themselves. A failed panel would show no image at all. A loose cable typically causes flickering or partial display, not uniform dimness. Review: Chapter 9, Laptop and Mobile Device Hardware (display technologies, backlight, inverter, LED driver, display troubleshooting).

When a driver update causes problems, use Device Manager's "Roll Back Driver" feature. Right-click the device → Properties → Driver tab → Roll Back Driver. This reverts to the previously installed driver version. The option is only available if a previous driver exists. If Roll Back is grayed out, you'll need to manually install an older driver version. Review: Chapter 12, Hardware and Network Troubleshooting (driver rollback, Device Manager, display troubleshooting).

ipconfig /release releases the current DHCP-assigned IP configuration. Follow this with ipconfig /renew to request a new IP from the DHCP server. This two-step process forces a fresh DHCP negotiation and often resolves APIPA (169.254.x.x) addressing issues caused by temporary DHCP communication failures. If /renew still gets an APIPA address, the DHCP server may be unreachable. Review: Chapter 6, Introduction to TCP/IP (ipconfig switches, DHCP troubleshooting, APIPA).

The correct procedure: (1) Clean all old thermal paste from both the CPU heat spreader and cooler base using 90%+ isopropyl alcohol and a lint-free cloth, (2) Apply a small pea-sized amount to the center of the CPU, (3) Seat the cooler with even pressure. The mounting pressure spreads the paste into a thin, even layer. Too much paste acts as an insulator and can overflow onto components. Some aftermarket coolers come with pre-applied paste. Review: Chapter 1, Motherboards, Processors, and Memory (thermal management, thermal paste application, CPU cooler installation).
